description: Free full-length narrative plus 1-page NCMHCE answer strategy cheat sheet for lead capture and product preview.

freeNarrative.title: Free Diagnostic Case — Tessa (Generalized Anxiety Disorder)
freeNarrative.presentingProblem:
You are a licensed mental health counselor in outpatient private practice. Your client self-referred after searching online for therapy late one night. She stated, "I’m not in crisis exactly. I’m just exhausted from being myself."

The client is a 29-year-old marketing project manager who reported chronic, difficult-to-control worry across multiple areas of her life, including work performance, her upcoming wedding, her father’s health, finances, and whether people are disappointed in her. She stated, "My brain acts like every problem is urgent and every mistake is permanent." She reported that this pattern has been present since adolescence but has worsened over the past eight months after being promoted into a role that involves supervising others.

She now checks emails repeatedly before sending them, rereads Slack messages to see whether she sounded rude, and mentally replays meetings at night. She stated, "If my boss says, 'Can we talk tomorrow,' I assume I’m getting fired. Then I spend twelve hours preparing for every possible disaster." She reported fatigue, irritability, muscle tension in her shoulders and jaw, difficulty concentrating, restlessness, and sleep disturbance. She stated that she can fall asleep but wakes around 3:00 a.m. thinking about unfinished tasks or possible future problems.

She reported feeling embarrassed that she appears competent externally while feeling "like a fraud with a nervous system problem" internally. Her fiancé has encouraged therapy because she becomes tearful, snappy, and withdrawn during periods of high stress. She denied panic attacks, though she described several moments of feeling "right on the edge of losing it" during which her chest feels tight and she fears she may cry at work. When asked what she means by "losing it," she stated, "Not like I’m going to hurt myself or someone else. More like I’m going to stop being able to keep all the plates spinning and everyone will see I’m not okay."

She denied any history of self-harm, suicide attempts, mania, psychosis, or substance misuse. She drinks one to two glasses of wine on weekends and denied other substances. She denied trauma history beyond what she described as growing up with a father who was loving but unpredictable because of untreated diabetes and periodic hospitalizations. She stated, "I learned early that if I stayed prepared, things felt less scary."

She reported that her mother was "a worrier too" and often asked her as a child whether doors were locked, assignments were done, or if something bad might happen to her father. The client stated that friends describe her as dependable, organized, and driven, but she experiences those same qualities as "fear dressed up as competence." She came to treatment now because she is tired of feeling physically tense all the time and because she worries that marriage, future parenthood, and increasing work responsibility will make her symptoms worse.
freeNarrative.mentalStatusObservation:
Your client presented in neat business attire and appeared her stated age. She was alert and fully oriented to person, place, time, and situation. Grooming and hygiene were good. Eye contact was consistent. Speech was clear, coherent, and mildly fast at times, especially when discussing work stress. Mood was reported as "stressed all the time." Affect was anxious but appropriate and reactive. Psychomotor activity was notable for fidgeting with her ring and periodically rubbing the back of her neck.

Thought processes were linear, logical, and goal-directed, though notably preoccupied with future-oriented worry. Thought content reflected fear of failure, perfectionism, and anticipatory anxiety. There was no evidence of delusions, hallucinations, or formal thought disorder. She denied current suicidal or homicidal ideation. Insight was fair to good; she recognized that her worry is excessive but reported feeling unable to shut it off. Judgment appeared intact. She denied substance misuse. She reported chronic shoulder tension, jaw clenching, headaches, and nonrestorative sleep but no acute medical concerns.
freeNarrative.familyHistory: The client is the older of two daughters. She described her mother as loving, highly responsible, and chronically anxious, though never formally diagnosed. Her father is a retired electrician with longstanding diabetes that was poorly managed during the client’s childhood, resulting in several frightening hospitalizations. She reported that the family often organized itself around preventing crises. She described no family history of bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, or completed suicide. Her younger sister has seen a therapist for panic symptoms in college. The client remains close with both parents and her sister, though she often feels cast in the role of "the capable one."
freeNarrative.workHistory: The client earned a bachelor’s degree in communications and has worked in marketing and project coordination roles for the past seven years. She was promoted eight months ago to project manager at a mid-sized healthcare technology company. She supervises three direct reports and coordinates deadlines across multiple departments. Her performance reviews have been strong, but she reported spending excessive time checking work, preparing for unlikely problems, and trying to anticipate others’ needs. She has not disclosed mental health concerns at work and worries that doing so would make her appear weak or incapable.
freeNarrative.intakeSessionSummary:
You completed a thorough intake and administered the GAD-7, on which the client scored 16, consistent with severe anxiety symptoms. You also administered the PHQ-9, on which she scored 9, reflecting mild depressive symptoms likely secondary to chronic anxiety and poor sleep. You conducted a direct risk assessment in response to her statement about feeling near the edge of "losing it"; she denied suicidal ideation, self-harm urges, homicidal ideation, and history of attempts.

You discussed the diagnosis of Generalized Anxiety Disorder and reviewed evidence-based treatment options, including CBT, worry monitoring, cognitive restructuring, behavioral experiments, and relaxation training. You normalized that high-functioning anxiety can still create meaningful impairment and physical distress. The client expressed relief at feeling understood and stated, "I thought therapy might tell me to just calm down better. This feels more specific than that." You scheduled weekly sessions and provided a worry log for the week.

questions.stem: When the client says she feels close to 'losing it,' she spontaneously clarifies she does not mean hurting herself or anyone else, but rather 'losing the ability to keep all the plates spinning.' What should the counselor do FIRST?
options: Ask a structured suicide risk assessment using a validated screener since any 'losing it' language warrants formal screening
Reflect the meaning she just offered and ask her to describe what 'losing it' looks like in her body and behavior in those moments
Move directly into teaching a grounding exercise so she has a coping tool before leaving the session
Document her denial of suicidal and homicidal ideation and proceed with the rest of the intake
questions.explanation: Best (B): The client has already volunteered that she is not describing suicidal or homicidal intent. The next NCMHCE-aligned step is to deepen understanding of what she actually means functionally and somatically before pivoting to assessment instruments or skills. Second-best (A): A formal screener is appropriate later, but jumping straight to it after she has clarified she is not suicidal can feel dismissive and misses clinical nuance. (C) Skills-first skips assessment and rapport. (D) Closing out the safety thread on a denial alone is premature documentation, not clinical care.

questions.stem: The client states, 'I’m exhausted from being myself.' Which response best balances empathy with clinical depth?
options: What has it been like carrying this level of tension for so long?
It sounds like the version of you that other people see is not the version you actually live with.
That’s a really powerful statement — say more about what you mean.
I hear how tired you are. We can work on building you a more sustainable pace.
questions.explanation: Best (B): A complex reflection names the gap between her external presentation and internal experience, which is the meaning she is actually pointing to. Second-best (A): A solid open question, but it stays at the level of duration and tension rather than meaning. (C) Generic prompt without reflection — common but shallow. (D) Pivots to problem-solving before her statement has been received.

questions.stem: Which DSM-5-TR diagnosis BEST fits the client’s presentation, and what is the strongest reason to favor it over a close differential?
options: Generalized Anxiety Disorder, because her worry is excessive, difficult to control, present more days than not for years across multiple domains, and accompanied by the required physical symptoms
Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder, because her checking emails and rereading messages function as compulsions tied to intrusive fears
Adjustment Disorder with Anxiety, because symptoms intensified after the work promotion eight months ago
Illness Anxiety Disorder, because much of her worry centers on her father’s health
questions.explanation: Best (A): Worry is diffuse, chronic since adolescence, ego-dystonic, and meets the GAD physical-symptom threshold (fatigue, muscle tension, sleep disturbance, irritability, restlessness, concentration). Second-best (C): The promotion is a real stressor, but Adjustment Disorder requires symptoms not better explained by another disorder — and her pattern predates the stressor by more than a decade, which rules it out. (B) Her checking is anxiety-driven worry behavior, not ego-dystonic obsessions paired with ritualized compulsions. (D) Her health-related worry is one of many themes, not the pervasive somatic preoccupation IAD requires.

questions.stem: Which treatment plan element should be sequenced FIRST in this client’s CBT for GAD?
options: Cognitive restructuring of catastrophic thoughts about being fired
Behavioral experiments around sending unchecked emails at work
Psychoeducation about the worry cycle and collaborative worry monitoring with a daily log
Applied relaxation training and diaphragmatic breathing
questions.explanation: Best (C): Evidence-based CBT for GAD begins with psychoeducation and self-monitoring so the client can identify her own triggers, themes, and maintaining patterns before active intervention. Second-best (D): Relaxation is a legitimate early CBT component but, without monitoring first, the client cannot tell when or why to apply it. (A) and (B) are appropriate later interventions, but cognitive restructuring and behavioral experiments require baseline data the worry log will produce.

questions.stem: The client reports replaying conversations at night to check whether she sounded rude. This is BEST conceptualized as:
options: A compulsion that should be targeted with exposure and response prevention
Post-event processing functioning as a covert checking behavior that maintains anxiety
Normal conscientiousness that does not require clinical intervention
A depressive ruminative style consistent with comorbid MDD
questions.explanation: Best (B): Post-event mental review is a well-documented anxiety-maintaining process — it provides short-term reassurance while reinforcing the belief that vigilance prevents harm. Second-best (A): Conceptually adjacent and ERP-informed strategies can help, but framing it as an OCD compulsion overpathologizes and points to the wrong protocol. (C) Minimizes clinically significant impairment. (D) Depressive rumination is past- and self-focused on loss/worthlessness, not future- and evaluation-focused like hers.

sections.sectionNarrative:
Your client arrived on time and completed the worry log consistently. Her GAD-7 this week is 13, down from 16 at intake. She reported that identifying her worry themes has been helpful but also "humbling" because she had not realized how often she catastrophizes. She stated, "I can turn literally anything into a five-step disaster scenario in under thirty seconds."

She described one recent example: her fiancé did not answer a text for two hours while at work, and she went from mild concern to imagining he had been in a car accident or had changed his mind about their relationship. By the time he called back, she was angry, tearful, and ashamed. She stated, "He was just in a meeting. I acted like I had survived a crisis that never happened."

She also reported increased awareness of how much reassurance she seeks from others, especially her fiancé and her mother. She asks whether they are upset, whether things are okay, and whether she handled situations correctly. She stated, "It helps for ten minutes, then I need it again."

At work, she has begun experimenting with sending emails after one review instead of four and has found that "nothing catastrophic happened," though she still feels highly tense when doing it. She asked you directly, "How do I stop needing certainty all the time? Because I know that’s what I’m really chasing."

questions.stem: The client asks how to stop needing certainty all the time. Which intervention BEST targets the underlying mechanism?
options: Teach progressive muscle relaxation so she can lower physiological arousal when uncertainty arises
Use Socratic questioning to dispute the evidence behind each individual catastrophic prediction
Plan graduated, in-vivo experiments in which she deliberately tolerates uncertainty without reassurance-seeking and tracks the actual outcome
Schedule daily worry time so she contains the worry to a defined window
questions.explanation: Best (C): Intolerance of uncertainty is the transdiagnostic core of GAD; behavioral experiments that deliberately approach uncertain situations without safety behaviors directly retrain the threat response. Second-best (B): Cognitive disputation helps with content but tends to become its own form of reassurance-seeking when uncertainty is the real driver. (A) and (D) are useful adjuncts but address symptoms, not the mechanism.

questions.stem: Reassurance from her fiancé relieves her anxiety for ten minutes, then it returns. From a behavioral standpoint, this pattern is BEST explained as:
options: Negative reinforcement of reassurance-seeking, which strengthens the behavior and maintains the anxiety cycle
Positive reinforcement, because the fiancé’s warm response makes her feel loved
Habituation failure caused by the anxiety being too intense to extinguish
Evidence that her anxiety has shifted from cognitive to interpersonal in nature
questions.explanation: Best (A): Reassurance removes an aversive state (uncertainty), so the behavior that produced relief (asking) is negatively reinforced and recurs more often. Second-best (C): Habituation language is in the right family but misnames the mechanism — the issue is reinforcement of avoidance, not failed extinction. (B) Confuses operant categories. (D) Mislabels a maintaining process as a diagnostic shift.

questions.stem: The client says, 'I acted like I survived a crisis that never happened.' Which response best supports therapeutic depth without colluding with self-criticism?
options: What was happening inside you in those two hours before he called back?
It sounds like part of you is harsh with the part of you that was scared.
That reaction makes sense given how anxiety hijacks the brain.
Let’s map that two-hour spiral on a thought record so we can see the chain.
questions.explanation: Best (B): Names the internal split between her self-critical voice and the frightened part — this is depth-oriented and counters shame without minimizing. Second-best (A): A strong open question, but stays at the level of content rather than the self-to-self relationship she just revealed. (C) Educates and normalizes but bypasses the affect. (D) Useful CBT tool, but pivots to technique before the moment is metabolized.

questions.stem: She has begun sending work emails after one review instead of four. From a CBT standpoint, this is MOST accurately described as:
options: Exposure with response prevention targeting a checking compulsion
A behavioral experiment that tests her catastrophic prediction by reducing a safety behavior
Behavioral activation aimed at reducing avoidance and increasing reinforcement
Stimulus control to limit the cues that trigger her anxiety
questions.explanation: Best (B): Behavioral experiments in CBT for GAD specifically test a predicted catastrophe by deliberately dropping a safety behavior (re-checking) and observing the actual outcome. Second-best (A): Mechanically similar, but ERP belongs to OCD protocols — the framing matters because rationale, dose, and homework instructions differ. (C) Behavioral activation is for depression. (D) Stimulus control is a sleep/habit technique, not what is happening here.

questions.stem: The client’s fiancé emails you directly asking 'how can I best support her between sessions?' What is the MOST appropriate next step under the ACA Code of Ethics?
options: Send a brief, generic reply with publicly available psychoeducation about anxiety so you do not disclose anything client-specific
Do not respond to the email; raise the contact with the client at the next session and let her decide whether and how to involve him, then obtain a written release before any further communication
Acknowledge receipt of the email, decline to discuss the client, and invite him to a joint session so collaboration can happen transparently
Forward the email to the client so she knows he reached out and can reply herself
questions.explanation: Best (B): Confidentiality means even acknowledging the therapeutic relationship requires consent. The clinically and ethically clean move is to bring the contact to the client, let her direct the response, and obtain a written release before any substantive exchange. Second-best (C): Inviting him to a joint session still presupposes acknowledgment of treatment and skips the consent step. (A) Generic content sent from your professional address still confirms a relationship. (D) Forwarding without prior conversation can feel intrusive and shifts a clinical decision onto the client without framing.

sections.sectionNarrative:
Your client arrived for her tenth session reporting meaningful improvement. Her GAD-7 score is now 8. She stated, "I still worry, but it doesn’t run the whole day anymore." She has been sleeping better on most nights and reports fewer headaches and less jaw tension.

She described a recent success: her supervisor scheduled a last-minute meeting, and although she noticed the familiar thought that she might be in trouble, she used the cognitive and behavioral strategies you had practiced rather than spiraling into all-night worry. The meeting turned out to be about a new project lead opportunity.

She also reported a more difficult moment from the previous weekend. Her father had a hypoglycemic episode at home and briefly scared the family. The client noticed herself immediately reverting to old roles — taking charge, overfunctioning, and mentally preparing for every possible medical outcome. She stated, "For two days it felt like I was fourteen again and the whole job was to hold everything together."

She was able to notice the pattern, name it, and use paced breathing and scheduled worry time, but she felt discouraged that the old intensity returned so quickly. She asked, "Does this mean I’m back at square one whenever real life happens?"

questions.stem: She asks whether her symptom spike means she is 'back at square one.' Which response is MOST therapeutic?
options: Setbacks are a normal part of recovery and don’t erase the work you’ve done.
Notice that you recognized the pattern, named it, and used your skills — that’s very different from where you were at intake.
What would it mean about you if it did mean you were back at square one?
Let’s look at the data: your GAD-7 dropped from 16 to 8, which objectively shows progress.
questions.explanation: Best (B): Reflects observable, behavioral evidence of skill use, which directly disconfirms the 'back at square one' belief and builds self-efficacy without reassuring her out of her feeling. Second-best (C): A meaningful exploratory question, but in this moment she is asking for orientation, not deeper interpretation of her catastrophizing. (A) True but generic — slides toward reassurance. (D) Score-based reassurance can feel invalidating when the client is reporting an emotional setback.

questions.stem: Her response to her father’s hypoglycemic episode is BEST conceptualized as:
options: A trauma response indicating that PTSD criteria should now be reassessed
State-dependent reactivation of an early family role under a salient cue, not a return of the underlying disorder
Evidence that the treatment plan needs to address codependency as a primary issue
A normal stress response that does not warrant clinical attention
questions.explanation: Best (B): A familiar cue (father’s medical crisis) triggered an old, well-rehearsed family role of overfunctioning. Naming it as cue-driven and role-based — rather than as relapse — is what enables relapse-prevention work. Second-best (D): It is a stress response, but dismissing it as 'normal' misses the clinically rich material. (A) The episode does not meet PTSD Criterion A or symptom clusters. (C) 'Codependency' is not a DSM construct and reframes the case unnecessarily.

questions.stem: Given a GAD-7 of 8 and consistent skill use, what is the MOST appropriate next phase of treatment?
options: Begin spacing sessions and collaboratively build a written relapse-prevention plan that includes early-warning signs, high-risk situations, and a coping menu
Maintain weekly sessions until the GAD-7 is below 5 to ensure full remission before any change
Begin termination this session since she has met treatment goals
Add a second modality such as group therapy to consolidate gains
questions.explanation: Best (A): Mild-range GAD-7 with active skill use is the standard window to taper, formalize relapse prevention, and shift the client toward being her own therapist. Second-best (B): Defensible but over-treats — there is no evidence base requiring sub-clinical scores before tapering, and continued weekly contact can foster therapy dependence. (C) Skips relapse prevention entirely. (D) Adds intensity when the indication is to reduce it.

questions.stem: Which statement BEST captures the durable mechanism of change this client is internalizing?
options: Her worries were inaccurate and she has learned to think more realistically
Her relationship with uncertainty has shifted: she can notice the urge to control it and choose not to act on it
She has reduced her exposure to stressors that used to trigger her
She has built a stronger support system to help her contain her anxiety
questions.explanation: Best (B): The therapeutic target in GAD is the relationship to uncertainty and the urge to control it, not the content of any single worry. This is what generalizes across future stressors. Second-best (A): Cognitive accuracy improves, but framing change as 'thoughts were wrong' is brittle — the next real uncertainty will produce real risk, and 'wrong thoughts' framing collapses. (C) She has not reduced exposure; she has changed her response. (D) External support is helpful but is not the internal mechanism of change.

sections.heading: The Golden Rule
content: Safety -> Rapport -> Least Assumptive -> Within Scope

sections.heading: 4-Step Decision Framework
content: 1. Check safety first: suicidal ideation, homicidal ideation, psychosis, abuse, severe impairment, or medical risk move to the front.
2. Early in the case, prioritize reflection, clarification, and assessment over advice or interpretation.
3. If the client asks what to do, explore meaning and context before jumping to direction.
4. When two answers seem right, choose the one that is more exploratory, less assumptive, and more client-centered.

sections.heading: Most Common Test Traps
content: Missing safety because the client sounds calm or vague.
Jumping to diagnosis before enough information is gathered.
Choosing an answer that acts outside counselor scope.
Picking the answer that sounds most active instead of most clinically appropriate.

sections.heading: Rapid Pattern Recognition
content: GAD = chronic, diffuse worry across domains.
Panic Disorder = sudden surges of fear plus catastrophic interpretation of body sensations.
MDD = depressed mood and/or loss of interest with functional impairment.
Bipolar spectrum = episodic mood shifts, especially decreased need for sleep and increased energy.
PTSD = trauma exposure plus intrusion, avoidance, and threat-related symptoms.
OCD = obsessions plus compulsions aimed at reducing distress or preventing feared outcomes.

sections.heading: When Two Answers Both Look Good
content: Pick the answer that builds alliance, gathers more information, and stays inside the counselor’s role.
Avoid answers that overpromise, overinterpret, or skip steps.

sections.heading: Final Reminder
content: You are not trying to sound smart. You are trying to think like a careful, ethical, entry-level clinician.
